transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-21 15:00 UTC | Duration approx 45m | Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Aurora Eng Lead), Tom Alvarez (Aurora CTO), Priya Rao (Aurora Platform)

Summary: Quick SDK integration walkthrough focusing on Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth and env setup, Console demo for routes and the Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Customer wants low-latency inference for chat features, interested in Dedicated vs hosted for data residency. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics: SDK quickstart (Python + TS), API key auth vs SSO, env vars and container setup, sample code for streaming, Console walkthrough (routes + rollouts), Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching/cache/quantization), security questions (SOC2, KMS, VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, and with me is Samir our SE. How's it going, Maya?
[00:08] Maya: Good, thanks. Sorry running a touch late, traffic in the south bay, but ready.
[00:12] Tom: Hey all, Tom here. We'll keep this high level and then dig into the SDK part.
[00:18] Samir: Great. Quick agenda: we'll show the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns, how to wire env vars and containers, then jump into the Console and Optimize tips for lower token cost and latency.
[00:28] Priya: Sounds good, main thing for us is set up by end of month and figure out whether Hosted covers our SLA or we need Dedicated. Also we have strict KMS + VPC rules.
[00:36] Lena: Totally, we'll cover that.

[00:45] [01:00] Samir: Ok opening the Python quickstart repo, this is the standard pattern: pip install redwood-inference (note: transcript may have package name slightly off), set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then call client.generate or client.chat with streaming. Here's sample snippet, sorry if the copy/paste in the shared deck looks a bit mashed.
[01:20] Maya: Can you show TypeScript too? Our front end team uses TS heavily.
[01:25] Samir: Yeah for TS we have the @redwood/inference SDK, npm install, set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or use the server-side secret manager. Example: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); then client.chat.stream(...) — the streaming example uses EventSource style, we also show WebSocket if you need low latency.
[01:40] Maya: When you say api key, does that mean anyone with the key can hit production? We use SSO for developer access internally.
[01:48] Lena: Good question — auth patterns: for quickstarts we show API key for simplicity. For production we recommend issuing short-lived tokens via your auth provider + Redwood's token exchange, or using our SAML/SSO integrations for Console access. For API-level calls from services, we support KMS-encrypted secrets in your vault, and you can do per-route tokens with RBAC.
[02:10] Tom: How does that work with our KMS? We use AWS KMS and need HSM-backed keys for some models.
[02:16] Samir: We integrate with customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, and for Hosted we offer encryption at rest with KMS-managed keys; for Dedicated/Private we can support bring-your-own KMS/HSM. There was a note in the security deck — we'll share the KMS integration guide after.

[02:35] [03:00] Priya: Walk me through env setup for containers. Our deploy pipeline is Docker -> ECS Fargate.
[03:05] Samir: Sure. Two options: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an ECS secret or reference it from Secrets Manager and pass to container via env var. If you're using Private with VPC peering, you'll also configure the endpoint and CA cert in REDWOOD_ENDPOINT and REDWOOD_CA — those names are in the quickstart README. Also consider short-lived tokens if multiple services are calling.
[03:30] Maya: Are there rate limits we should be aware of?
[03:34] Lena: Hosted has default quotas; we can increase for enterprise customers. Dedicated gives you reserved throughput and predictable SLOs. For the POC we can provision a small Dedicated pool to run your benchmarks.

[03:50] [04:20] Samir: Okay let's demo a Python streaming call. (sound of screen share) Example uses client.chat.stream and yields partial tokens every ~200ms. There may be a slight dip in the transcript here, the streaming examples are in the quickstart repo.
[04:45] Maya: Looks straightforward. How about model selection and latency tradeoffs? We want sub-200ms median token latency for short prompts.
[04:55] Samir: For sub-200ms you're probably looking at smaller, optimized variants or using Dedicated pools on appropriate GPU family. Our Runtime does kernel selection and continuous batching. Also Optimize suggests batching parameters and quantization profiles. For chat with short history we recommend prefix/KV cache enabled and a batch size tuned to your RPS distribution.
[05:20] Tom: What's the overhead of KV cache invalidation? We can have many rapid ephemeral conversations.
[05:26] Samir: KV cache is per-session; if conversations are ephemeral you might skip long-lived cache, but prefix caching still helps. There's a small memory tradeoff; we'll share bench numbers.

[05:45] [06:10] Priya: Can we see the Console? We want to understand routes, rollouts and observability.
[06:15] Lena: Yep sharing Console (note: the UI name was transcribed as 'Redwood infer console' earlier). On the left are Routes — you can map an API route to a model variant, set per-route batching and fallback policies. Rollouts: Canary and A/B are supported, and you can set automatic fallback to cheaper variants if latency spikes.
[06:40] Samir: Tracing and token-level cost breakdowns are under Observability. You can see per-request token counts and per-route latency percentiles, which we find super helpful during POC.

[07:05] [07:55] Maya: Security — we need audit logs and SSO for Console, and logs retained for 12 months. Is that supported?
[08:00] Lena: Yes. Audit logs are available and retention is configurable as an add-on. SSO via SAML/Okta is supported and RBAC can be mapped to your groups. For compliance we have SOC2 and ISO docs which we'll share.

[08:20] [09:00] Tom: Bandwidth/cost question — our CFO wants a clear cost story: tokens x unit price + infra for Dedicated. Any tooling to estimate?
[09:08] Samir: The Console has a cost estimator and we have Optimize which gives model/quantization recommendations and batching suggestions to reduce unit token cost. For example, switching to 8-bit quantization on certain models typically reduces GPU memory and cost 20-30% with some quality tradeoffs — we can run quality regressions on your prompt set.

[09:40] [10:15] Maya: About the quickstart code: can it run locally or does it assume network access to Redwood hosted endpoints? We have some air-gapped testing needs.
[10:22] Samir: Quickstarts assume network access to the control plane. For air-gapped/on-prem we have a Private option where the control plane is customer-managed and the inference can run in your network. We'll send the Private deployment guide.

[10:40] [11:05] (brief cross-talk, someone drops a link)
[11:10] Samir: Back to code — here's a sample streaming TS handler to forward tokens to the browser. (reads code) One caveat: don't embed API keys in client-side code; always proxy through your backend.
[11:30] Maya: We'll need example for refresh tokens and short-lived credentials.
[11:35] Lena: We'll include an example auth flow: users authenticate to your auth provider, server exchanges for a short Redwood token which is limited to a route and TTL.

[11:50] [12:30] Priya: For the POC, we want to run a benchmark: 1k users sim, three prompt patterns, measure p95 latency and cost. Can you provide a benchmark script?
[12:38] Samir: Yup — I'll share a JMeter/small Python load script and recommended batch sizes. We'll also recommend model variants to test.

[12:55] [13:20] Tom: Who else on your side should we coordinate with for networking?
[13:24] Lena: Samir is primary for the SE bench run, and our Solutions Eng team for Dedicated provisioning. I'll put you in touch with our infra PM if you decide on Dedicated.

[13:40] [14:10] Maya: Any callouts about pitfalls? We've spoken to other vendors and they had surprises around tokenization and newline handling in logs.
[14:18] Samir: Tokenization differences are model-specific. We include tokenization tools in the SDK and Console shows raw token counts. Regarding logs, we redact PII by default for hosted but for Private you'll have control.

[14:40] [15:05] Priya: Can Redwood do pre-warming or reserved capacity for big launches?
[15:10] Lena: Yes, for Dedicated we can reserve capacity and configure autoscaling with warm-up policies. We'll include the SLA doc with latency/availability targets.

[15:30] [16:00] (short pause while Lena shares links in chat)
[16:05] Maya: Thanks — seeing the Console makes it easier. Next steps for us: run quickstart locally, then choose POC model list and run bench.
[16:14] Lena: Great recap. I'll send quickstart links, security docs and the benchmark script. Samir will follow up on batch/quantization recommended settings.

[16:30] [17:00] Tom: One last question — any out-of-the-box eval tooling to guard against regressions?
[17:06] Samir: Yes Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to eval sets, you can set regression alerts and tie to rollout policies.

[17:20] Lena: Alright, thanks everyone. Quick recap of action items in chat. We'll follow up with pricing and trial Dedicated options.
[17:30] Maya: Thanks.
[17:32] Tom: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
